paragraphs: The following judgments concern media programming directors' daily work planning and scheduling radio/television programming and event coverage, directing and coordinating news, sports, and production staff, and checking program logs for compliance; they do not predict hiring, qualifications, broadcast permissions, or ultimate responsibility.

Media programming directors plan radio/television programming and event coverage schedules, coordinate news, sports, and production staff, monitor program quality and logs, select material, and obtain usage permissions as needed. US O*NET tasks include checking program logs under FCC rules. This does not make FCC rules applicable in China, nor does the occupational title imply that one individual bears all ultimate responsibility for content, copyright, and site safety. Specific duties depend on organizational authorization.

60-minute paper exercise (entirely fictional, with no real broadcasting): Monday through Friday, fill 18:00—18:30 each day with 30 minutes of non-overlapping programming under the exercise's internal rules, using A once, B once, and D once daily. A is 10 minutes of verified community news; B is 12 minutes of verified sports reporting; D is an 8-minute filler short. Permissions for all three explicitly cover this fictional station once daily Monday through Friday. C is a 15-minute music segment with permission pending and cannot be scheduled. Of 100 fictional preference records, 60 choose community news and 40 sports. Use these only to explain ordering, not predict ratings. Deliver a five-day start/end timetable, permission checklist, and anomaly record. Anomaly input: Tuesday's log records A18:00—18:10, B18:10—18:23, and D18:23—18:31. Mark differences from the draft; do not change actual logs to scheduled times. Spend the first 10 minutes reading, 25 minutes scheduling, 15 minutes independently checking calculations, and the final 10 minutes recording questions for an authorized person. These internal rules are neither FCC nor Chinese regulations.

Reference deliverable (hide before answering): all five days use A18:00—18:10, B18:10—18:22, and D18:22—18:30; 10+12+8=30 minutes, with no gaps or overlaps. Do not use C while permission is pending. The 60 / 40 preferences may explain A before B but do not imply actual ratings. On Tuesday, B lasts 1 minute longer than drafted, D shifts 1 minute later, and the 18:31 finish exceeds the window by 1 minute. Preserve the actual anomaly record and report causes and impacts to an authorized person; do not falsify logs or independently claim compliance. The work sample needs the draft, permissions and pending items, log differences, one corrected error, and questions about subsequent handling. It does not establish broadcast or copyright authorization.

This page covers O*NET 27-2012.03, Media Programming Directors: directing and coordinating staff engaged in scheduling radio/television programming and producing programs such as sports or news. Common reported titles include Broadcast Content Manager, News Director, Newscast Director, Production Director, Program Coordinator, Program Director, Program Manager, Programming Director, Station Manager, and Television Program Director. This page excludes adjacent occupations such as Chief Executives, General and Operations Managers, and Public Relations Managers.

entries: Inputs: broadcast time slots and durations, community needs, ratings and audience demographic data, programming and event material, news and sports content, budgets and staff schedules, and applicable rules such as FCC requirements and permission conditions.

Verifiable outputs: executable programming schedules and broadcast plans, content and quality review records, program logs and compliance checks, material permissions and expiration information, budget monitoring results, and event coverage and production coordination records.

Complete workflow: plan programming and event coverage around broadcast durations and time slots → assign work and coordinate departments → monitor and review schedules and program quality → check program logs and FCC compliance → evaluate and adjust programming using audience feedback → review, record, and hand over, completing the loop.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether time slots and durations are met; whether content sources have been verified; whether material has valid permission; whether logs match actual broadcasts and comply with rules such as FCC requirements; and whether commitments involving minors or guest contracts fall within authorization.

US O*NET survey: 100% use email daily, 78% have face-to-face discussions daily, and 82% work in controlled indoor environments daily; 57% usually work more than 40 hours a week, 49% face time pressure daily, and 56% consider accuracy extremely important. These are respondent percentages, not Chinese working hours or job guarantees.

Research inputs: O*NET27-2012.03 identity, tasks, context, ECA, and education concern the suboccupation; 2025 wages, 2025—2035 employment, and industries concern parent occupation Producers and Directors (27-2012). FCC tasks reflect US broadcasting and are not extrapolated to Chinese rules, qualifications, or industries.

Verify first: broadcast slots and durations, content sources and editorial guidelines, material permission scope and term, applicable rules such as FCC requirements, budgets and staff schedules, and content, copyright, and site safety judgments requiring an authorized person's confirmation.

Work cycle: begin with checking slots and requirements, proceed through programming and event planning, departmental coordination, schedule monitoring and quality review, program log and compliance checks, and end with evaluation and adjustment based on feedback. Do not broadcast unverified content, use material without permission, or proceed before safety or copyright questions are confirmed.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries: this page covers only radio/television programming and production coordination under 27-2012.03. Chief executives handle overall organizational strategy and ultimate responsibility; general and operations managers handle daily organizational operations; public relations managers handle external communication. Their objects of work, authorization, and responsibilities are not interchangeable.

Difference from chief executives: chief executives focus on overall organizational strategy, business results, and ultimate responsibility; this occupation focuses on specific programming schedules, content choices, and broadcast compliance, with responsibility for program outputs within organizational authorization.

Difference from general and operations managers: general and operations managers handle daily organizational operations and resource allocation; this occupation focuses on programming and event coverage schedules, production coordination, and content compliance.

Difference from public relations managers: public relations managers focus on external communication and brand messages; this occupation focuses on content planning, scheduling, and broadcast execution. Their objects of work and deliverables differ.

Difference from training and development managers: training and development managers focus on employee learning and capability development; this occupation focuses on programming and event coverage schedules and production coordination. Compare outputs and authorization.
Tasks and AI: media programming directors' task exposure to AI does not equal job replacement. Humans remain responsible for programming choices, copyright permissions, and broadcast judgments.

Editorial trial suggestion: try AI-assisted feedback organization, draft schedules, and lead retrieval using fictional material, then check durations, real sources, and permissions individually. O*NET Hot Technologies offers recruitment skill signals, not proof of widespread adoption of these generative AI tasks. Tools cannot issue material permissions or replace organizational authorization. AI Impact Score 58% is an editorial estimate. Model impact index for three equally weighted representative core tasks; not a measured share of working time or a job-loss probability. floor((75+75+25)/3+0.5)=58; fermatmind-ai-impact-v1; 2026-10-18.The three tasks, ratings and sources are listed in the FermatMind method source record on this page.
Evidence method: task capability, organizational adoption, and employment outcomes are three different kinds of evidence and require separate verification.
Differences across directions: AI-related changes and remaining responsibilities differ across schedule planning, content review, copyright management, and production coordination.
Responsibility process: from checking inputs and limiting tasks to human review, documentation, and escalation.
Usage boundary: tool outputs must be traceable to original time slots, ratings data, permission documents, and broadcast guidelines.
Editorial hypothesis: trial data organization or drafting with fictional feedback and licensed material. This does not mean this occupation's adoption rate has been measured.
Have the responsible person review schedules, content, and compliance judgments.

The human resources ministry's enterprise remuneration survey is classified by occupation or position and does not generate this occupation's median, percentiles, or stable monthly pay.

Verify actual pay periods, fixed pay, project remuneration, and benefits against the specific role and contract. This page has no Chinese pay-structure distribution for this occupation. Its title cannot establish widespread mixed annual, hourly, and project pay, and proxy figures are not used to fill gaps.

Industry wages provide broad context only, not a precise occupational median or starting pay. This page has not obtained an exact mapping between this US occupation and Chinese statistical categories and does not infer Chinese industry affiliation from US employer distributions.

Insufficient evidence: national occupational wages for media programming directors in mainland China were not obtained within this round's public scope. This page explicitly marks the gap and does not fill it with industry proxies or US figures.

BLS 2025 combined-scope wage data: median annual wage USD 90,360 (approximately USD 43.44 per hour); 10th percentile USD 45,780 (USD 22.01 per hour), 25th percentile USD 62,670 (USD 30.13 per hour), 75th percentile USD 134,800 (USD 64.81 per hour), and 90th percentile USD 198,540 (USD 95.45 per hour). These are O*NET's combined figures for Producers and Directors (27-2012), not this occupation separately. Percentiles are statistical positions and do not describe individual take-home income.

Wage distribution positions: these figures describe a US combined statistical distribution. Percentiles do not represent seniority or experience levels and cannot be interpreted as entry-level pay or guaranteed income.

Current O*NET parent-occupation industry shares: 46% information, 10% arts, entertainment, and recreation, 10% professional, scientific, and technical services, and 34% other industries. BLS separately provides 2025 wages for four detailed industries for the parent occupation, not programming directors separately; national percentiles are not substituted.

Parent occupation 27-2012: 181,000 employed in 2025, projected 188,300 in 2035, growth of 4% over 2025—2035 and a net increase of 7,300; 12,100 average annual openings include replacements. Employment includes self-employed people, while OEWS wages exclude them; these cannot be treated as the same wage sample. Parent-occupation figures are not separate occupational figures.

How to interpret these figures: explain employment levels, growth rates, net changes, and annual openings separately; they cannot be combined into an individual employment guarantee. Combined scope cannot replace a separately reported occupation. Industry and regional differences are substantial; do not extrapolate across regions.
Fit signals: assess media programming director fit through observable behavior, without substituting personality labels for tasks, qualifications, and responsibility judgments.

Direct answer: if you can balance content choices, schedule coordination, and compliance while accepting responsibility for broadcast results, further exploration is worthwhile. Otherwise, compare adjacent directions first.

Positive signals: making explainable content and scheduling judgments under time-slot and ratings pressure, willingness to coordinate across departments, and accepting responsibility for programming and broadcast results.

Reasons for caution: if responsibility for content and broadcast results is difficult or you lack patience for high-pressure scheduling and frequent coordination, consider adjacent directions or production roles first.
Trial action: complete a scheduling, content, and compliance exercise for an entirely fictional broadcast week, then decide whether to continue.

RIASEC (ECA): the interest code describes preferences for leadership and decisions (Enterprising), procedural handling of records and data (Conventional), and creative expression (Artistic). Use it only to generate hypotheses, not infer hiring or competence.

Editorial self-check: check whether 10+12+8 equals exactly 30 minutes, permissions cover once daily, and the actual extra 1 minute in the log is recorded truthfully. These behaviors can help explore accuracy and recording habits. Big Five labels cannot predict hiring or confer authorization.
Labels such as MBTI cannot determine competence. First check actual tasks, standards, and responsibility boundaries, then decide whether to continue.

Inaccurate content or statements: broadcasting before verifying sources means content has not been reviewed, potentially damaging credibility and prompting corrections or complaints. Controls include checking sources under editorial guidelines and recording correction procedures. Boundaries depend on internal guidelines and law.
Insufficient copyright permission: using material with inadequate scope, term, or territorial coverage may cause legal and authorization disputes. Confirm permission scope and term before use.

Program log or scheduling errors: logs differing from actual broadcasts may affect traceability and scheduling. Preserve actual records, investigate differences, and make authorized corrections under organizational procedures. O*NET's FCC reference is US task context, not a substitute for Chinese rules or specific FCC provisions.

Site and equipment safety: setting up remote facilities or working without confirming safety conditions may injure people or damage equipment. Confirm conditions under site safety procedures before working.

Common escalation rule: whenever content, copyright, site safety, or contract applicability is unclear, stop or isolate the relevant activity first. Submit facts, impacts, and unresolved questions to an authorized person for confirmation before continuing.

Practical entry point: entry-level media programming director samples use only public or fictional data to demonstrate scheduling understanding and content and compliance judgments. First confirm the role's first-year tasks and review methods.

O*NET respondents' education for this US suboccupation: 52% bachelor's degrees, 31% high school, and 15% some college without a degree. JobZone4 describes general preparation, not a uniform threshold or Chinese requirement. Chinese production and operation permits concern organizations conducting specified business, distinct from individual appointments, training, and material copyright.

Portfolio: complete this page's five-day, 30-minute schedule, A/B/D permission checklist, pending C item, and Tuesday log differences. Retain one error and correction and explain anomaly decisions requiring an authorized person. Do not submit real audience data, material, or contracts.

Separate organizational permits, individual appointments, and material copyright. Articles Two and Four of China's 2025 revised Provisions on the Administration of Radio and Television Program Production and Operation specify production and operation scope and organizational permits; Article Eleven exempts legally established radio and television stations from obtaining this additional permit. It is not an individual programming director license, a station establishment permit, or material authorization.

Editorial seven-day plan (30—60 minutes daily on paper): Day 1, read slots and permissions. Day 2, independently calculate start and end times for five days. Day 3, mark C as pending and explain ordering. Day 4, calculate Tuesday's actual log differences. Day 5, hide the reference, recalculate, and correct errors. Day 6, have a peer recalculate from the problem statement alone, then compare. Day 7, compile the draft, permission table, anomalies, corrections, and evidence for continuing or stopping. No real broadcasting.

Qualification decisions: O*NET certification and training directories help identify possible credentials and training opportunities. Certification does not equal broadcast permission, employer appointment, or ultimate responsibility. Credentials, hiring, and authorization are different states.

Capability ladder: before entering media programming direction, verify the official occupational scope, actual employer requirements, education or training, local rules, and supervised tasks. Do not infer these directly from adjacent occupations. Advancement rests on reviewable scheduling and compliance records, not a guaranteed number of years.

Transition path: before changing direction, list transferable skills in programming, content and compliance judgments, departmental coordination, and copyright and material management, alongside guidelines, permissions, and safety knowledge to acquire. Check each against adjacent roles' qualifications and responsibilities.

US parent occupation 27-2012: 181,000 employed in 2025, projected 188,300 in 2035, growth of 4% over 2025—2035, and net increase of 7,300; 12,100 average annual openings include replacements. Not programming directors separately, current recruitment, or individual success rates.
Employment levels, growth rates, net changes, and annual openings must be explained separately and cannot be combined into an individual employment guarantee.
Recruitment samples show demand only within the sampled time, region, and mix of roles; they are not national demand rates.
AI or technology research describes the scope for task assistance, not organizational adoption and still less net employment change.

Adjacent transitions: moving from media programming direction to producing and directing, art direction, film and video editing, or casting and talent direction requires checking differences in tools, qualifications, and responsibilities individually. Each path needs additional evidence corresponding to its new outputs.
